title: Why New Orleans players sounded alike: Noone, Ory and a piano-trumpet man
summary: Thomas discusses early New Orleans arpeggio-based playing, a Minneapolis trumpeter who copied Louis, clarinetists like Simeon and Noone, and Noone's praise of Kid Ory.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: In the early days, they just played the arpeggios, because they didn't get into the intricate things, like we do now, with the neighboring tones and all of that. They didn't get involved. They just played the melody. I copied more after them... Because I met a trumpet player in Minneapolis; I can't think of his name now. This guy could play piano and trumpet at the same time. He could accompany himself on piano and play trumpet.
I've seen guys do that.

And he used to copy all of Louis' solos. He could play 'em note for note. But he was just from New Orleans, and that beat was in him. Later on, I found out Fats Domino had that same thing. He had all them guys in New Orleans, he... Look at all the clarinet players. Simeon, Buster Bailey... [BUSTER BAILEY WAS FROM MEMPHIS]
Jimmie Noone. Don't forget Jimmie Noone.
Yeah, Jimmie Noone. Chicago. There were great musicians you know of in Chicago!
But Jimmie Noone wasn't born in Chicago.
No. But he used all... And he used to always rave about that trombone player...

Ory. Ory.
Kid Ory.
Kid Ory. He raved about him. He thought he was the greatest trombone player... And he used about every trombone player, every musician that was any good. I guess he had run out of musicians...
Well, Duke did the same thing later!
I guess he'd run out of musicians in Chicago, so he started picking... That's how he called Walter [sic: Wallace] Bishop and got that band.
Well, they say he didn't like it in Chicago because he'd only (?) with those New Orleans guys (?) up there.
Right.
